title: He Finished This the Year He Said Oil Paint Repelled Him, Then Barely Touched a Brush for Twenty
standfirst: In 1965 Constantin Flondor made this small copy after El Greco at almost the exact moment he began, by his own later account, to feel physical revulsion for painting in oil. Within a year he had co-founded a group built to argue painting out of the room entirely, and the record he left behind shows he mostly kept his word for the next two decades.

sections.heading: The Year His Own Catalogue Turns
sections.body: Wikiart's [chronological list](https://www.wikiart.org/en/constantin-flondor/all-works/text-list) of Constantin Flondor's work treats 1965 as a hinge. Four other pieces carry that same year — *The Marvelous Seed*, *The Joy of Living*, and two canvases under a Romanian title that translates roughly as "that we enter to feast" — and together with this one they are the last cluster on the list that looks like what the word painting usually means. What follows in 1966 and 1967 is still titled like landscape at first, but the list fills fast with "studies," "energy fields," and "unstable compositions," and by 1968 anything resembling a finished picture has all but stopped. It is worth setting against the artist's [own Wikiart overview](https://www.wikiart.org/en/constantin-flondor), where the three movements attached to his entire career are Abstract Art, Op Art, and Contemporary. Expressionism, the label stamped on this one canvas, does not appear anywhere else in it — and the painting's own [catalogue entry](https://www.wikiart.org/en/constantin-flondor/d-apr-s-el-greco-1965) complicates that single label further, filing it under Expressionism while its own breadcrumb trail runs it through Abstract Art too, for a picture whose genre tag is simply Figurative.

sections.heading: He Called the Technique Itself Repulsive
sections.body: The fullest account of what happened next turns up, oddly, in a [2010 auction catalogue](https://harmonious-dream-ha5-efahrfwj.on-forge.com/en/auction/licitatia-de-primavara-10-2010-1/lot/studiu-de-energie-en-37632) written for a charcoal study made two years after this painting. It describes Flondor beginning, starting in 1965, to deliberately give up oil paint, and renders his own reasoning as "repulsie pentru tehnica în ulei" — repulsion for the oil technique itself, which he found slow, heavy, and suffocating. The same entry has him reading Paul Klee's pedagogical writings for the first time that year, discussed with Ştefan Bertalan and Roman Cotoșman inside the circle that would shortly become a formal group, and sitting in on bionics seminars that a Professor Eduard Pamfil was running in Timișoara. None of that is the frame of mind that produces a careful copy after a sixteenth-century altarpiece painter — which makes it worth noticing that this picture and that frame of mind belong to the same twelve months.

sections.heading: A Group Founded to Argue Against "Predominant Figurativism"
sections.body: In 1966 Flondor, Bertalan, and Cotoșman formally founded the group that would become known as 111, growing out of the Timișoara art lyceum where Flondor taught and, from 1969, served as director. [Revista 22's account](https://revista22.ro/cultura/grupurile-111-sigma) of the group's early programme describes its aim as moving past "figurativismul predominant" — predominant figurativism — toward a visual language built on cybernetics, structuralism, and mathematics, discussed alongside the op-art experiments of Vasarely, Agam, and Soto. The group represented Romania at the 1969 Constructivist Biennale in Nuremberg; not long after, with Cotoșman's departure first for Germany and then the United States, it reorganised as Sigma. A standing project at the [National Museum of Art in Timișoara](https://mnart.museum/en/project/utopia-and-research-timisoara-experimental-groups-111-and-sigma-1966-1981/) now treats both groups as a single continuous research programme, interdisciplinary by design, that pushed toward urban-scale structures the city itself never built.

sections.heading: What "After El Greco" Doesn't Say
sections.body: Flondor's own catalogue gives this picture nothing beyond a title and a year: no medium is recorded, no dimensions, no note on which El Greco he had in mind. Romania does hold genuine ones. The National Museum of Art's collection includes three El Grecos inherited from King Carol I's former royal holdings, among them an [Adoration of the Shepherds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoration_of_the_Shepherds_%28El_Greco%2C_Bucharest%29) painted around 1596 for a Madrid altarpiece that was later broken up and sold piecemeal through nineteenth-century Paris, before a fragment of it reached the royal palace at Sinaia in 1879. Whether a young painter working in Timișoara in 1965 had that canvas in mind, a reproduction of it, or an entirely different El Greco altogether is not a question any source answers. On this particular work, the title is the only evidence there is, and the honest thing to do with thin evidence is say so rather than invent the rest.

sections.heading: The Nearest Hard Evidence: Charcoal, Not Oil
sections.body: The clearest material confirmation of what Flondor meant by "repulsion" sits in an unrelated sale rather than a monograph. That same [2010 auction lot](https://harmonious-dream-ha5-efahrfwj.on-forge.com/en/auction/licitatia-de-primavara-10-2010-1/lot/studiu-de-energie-en-37632) is a work titled *Studiu de energie*, signed and dated 1967, executed in charcoal on paper rather than paint, 60 by 85 centimetres. It carried an estimate of €1,000 to €1,500 and sold for €700. Two years after this small copy after El Greco, in other words, the artist who had been cataloguing "energy studies" had already swapped the brush for a stick of charcoal — precisely the shift the oil-repulsion story predicts, and recorded independently, in a sale room ledger rather than anything he wrote about himself.

sections.heading: Where the Catalogue Resumes, and Who Is Reading It Now
sections.body: On Wikiart's own record, nothing resembling a painting carries Flondor's name again until *Sky (11 April)* in 1985 — the better part of twenty years after this one. By then the group he had co-founded had become the subject of institutional attention rather than its own argument: besides the Timișoara museum's standing research project on 111 and Sigma, a 512-page monograph, [*When Eye Touches Cloud*](https://institutulprezentului.ro/en/publications/constantin-flondor-when-eye-touches-cloud/), appeared in 2021 to trace a single thread through seven decades of his output, from early paintings through kinetic art, land art, and photography. One later essay on his work insists that even his most geometric constructions [still answer to something observed in the plant world](https://institutulprezentului.ro/en/publications/constantin-flondor-the-gaze-that-rewrites-space/) — which suggests the referent he needed from nature never entirely left, even after the referent he once took from a four-hundred-year-old altarpiece painter did.
